text: Started on a folder that holds CSV and .xlsx files (also in subfolders), the home page lists every dataset found with its file name, sheet name for Excel, row count and column count.

GET /api/datasets/<id>/profile returns a JSON object mapping every column name to one of geospatial, temporal, categorical, numerical or other, and the same mapping is saved as a JSON file in the app's output folder.

Columns named lat, lon, lng, latitude or longitude (any case) are geospatial; date columns are temporal; integer and float columns are numerical; text columns with at most 50 distinct values and at most 50% distinct are categorical; other text columns are other.
A dataset with a temporal and a numerical column shows a time-series line chart of that numerical column over the temporal column on its dashboard page.
A dataset with a categorical and a numerical column shows a bar chart of the numerical column summed per category on its dashboard page.
A dataset with latitude and longitude columns shows a 3D map of its points, drawn as a Plotly 3D scatter, on its dashboard page; a dataset without them shows no map.
A dataset with no matching rule shows its column types and a table of its first rows and no charts, and the page loads without error.
Every dashboard page shows the dataset's column types and a table of its first 20 rows.
No page served by the app references a script, stylesheet, font or image on another host; every asset URL in the home and dashboard pages returns 200 from the app itself.
For a dataset with more rows than the map cap (default 50,000), the map data sent to the browser holds at most the cap and the page shows how many points are shown out of the total.
One launcher command, given a folder, starts the app on localhost and opens the dashboard home page in the default browser.
An empty or unreadable file in the folder is listed on the home page as could not be read, and the other datasets still list and open.
A Dockerfile and a Start-DataBoot.ps1 script are provided; the script checks Docker is running, mounts the chosen folder read-only, starts the container and opens the browser.
TSV, JSON, JSONL, GeoJSON and Parquet files in the folder are listed as datasets with their row and column counts, and a Parquet file gives the same column types and charts as the same data in CSV.

Files that are not a supported data type (for example .xls or .pdf) are listed in an Other files table on the home page with their type, size in bytes and modified date, without a link to a dashboard.

The charts API and dashboard page give a donut for a categorical column with 2 to 6 values, a histogram for a numerical column, a scatter and a correlation heatmap for two or more numerical columns, and a country map for a column of country names, with at most 8 charts per dataset.
Every chart on a dashboard page has exactly one rule caption and one count in the form 'N of M points' or 'N of M rows', and the page shows no other sentences.

Each dashboard offers XLSX and PPTX downloads; the XLSX opens in openpyxl with a first sheet named Data headed by the column names and at least one native chart, and the PPTX opens in python-pptx with a title slide plus one slide per chart, each holding a native chart.
The product is called DataBoot: the home page title and h1 read DataBoot, every dashboard title ends with ' - DataBoot', and no page says DataOS.
A .parquet file that cannot be read is listed on the home page as could not be read with its reason, and the other datasets still list and open.
Every count of 1,000 or more on the home and dashboard pages (rows, columns, bytes, N of M) is shown with thousands separators, for example 1,234 of 60,000.

On the home and dashboard pages each table's title (Datasets, Could not be read, Other files, Columns, First rows) is an h2 heading inside the table caption, and column headers show the column names in their original case.

requirements.txt lists xlsxwriter==3.3.0, python-pptx==1.0.2, openpyxl==3.1.5 and pyarrow==26.0.0, and the repository vendors none of these libraries; an XLSX exported by the app reopens in openpyxl without a 'no default style' warning.
On a dashboard page the Plotly tool bar of each chart is visible without hovering, and its buttons can be reached with the Tab key.

When one sheet of an Excel workbook cannot be read, the "Could not be read" table on the home page lists it as the file name and sheet (for example book.xlsx - Lookup), and the other sheets of that workbook still list and open as datasets.
A .json or .jsonl file that is not valid JSON is listed as could not be read with the note "invalid JSON"; valid JSON that is not a list of records keeps the note "not a list of records".
The country map lists countries sorted by value, largest first, like the bar chart; the 3D map titles its z axis and colour bar with the name of the z column.

Start-DataBoot.ps1 creates the venv with the newest Python from 3.11 to 3.13 it finds: it tries py -3.13, py -3.12 and py -3.11 in that order, then python only when that python reports a version from 3.11 to 3.13, so a machine with Python 3.12 and 3.14 and no 3.11 gets a 3.12 venv.

When no Python 3.11 to 3.13 is found, or venv creation or a pip install returns a non-zero exit code, Start-DataBoot.ps1 prints a message naming the failed step, deletes the partial .venv folder, waits for a key press so the window stays open, and exits with code 1 instead of running .venv\Scripts\python.exe.
A test fails if Start-DataBoot.ps1 creates the venv with one hardcoded Python version (for example only py -3.11) instead of trying 3.13, 3.12 and 3.11.

When one sheet's XML in an Excel workbook is corrupt (truncated or not XML), the other sheets of that workbook still list and open as datasets, and the corrupt sheet is listed under "Could not be read" with its sheet name (for example book.xlsx - Bad) and the note "not a valid xlsx".
